body:
From Delhi's province to an independent kingdom

During the 14th century, Gujarat was governed as a province of the Delhi Sultanate. Its fertile agricultural lands, established towns and access to the Arabian Sea made it economically important. However, the weakening of central authority in Delhi allowed several provincial governors to establish independent kingdoms.

The Gujarat Sultanate emerged from this political change. It became a regional kingdom ruled by its own sultans, with a government, military establishment and sources of revenue based in Gujarat.

A sultanate is a state ruled by a sultan. The Gujarat Sultanate was an independent regional sultanate, distinct from the Delhi Sultanate, although it developed from territory previously governed under Delhi's authority.

The rulers and events that established the kingdom

Muzaffar Shah I: Establishment of independent rule

Zafar Khan, who had served as governor of Gujarat under Delhi, asserted independent authority and assumed the title Muzaffar Shah I in 1407. He is generally identified as the founder of the independent Gujarat Sultanate.

The distinction between the founder of the kingdom and the founder of Ahmedabad is important. Muzaffar Shah I established independent dynastic rule, while his successor Ahmad Shah I founded Ahmedabad as a new capital.

Ahmad Shah I: Foundation of Ahmedabad

Ahmad Shah I, also written as Ahmed Shah I, ruled from 1411 to 1442. In 1411, he founded Ahmedabad on the eastern bank of the Sabarmati River. The new capital became an important centre of government, military authority, commerce and architecture.

Mahmud Begada: Consolidation and expansion

Mahmud Shah I, commonly known as Mahmud Begada, ruled from approximately 1458 to 1511. His reign is especially associated with the conquest of Junagadh in 1472 and the capture of Pavagadh near Champaner in 1484. Following the latter conquest, he developed Champaner into an important royal capital.

End of independent Sultanate rule

The independent kingdom continued after Mahmud Begada. In 1573, the Mughal emperor Akbar incorporated Gujarat into the Mughal Empire. This marked the end of the Gujarat Sultanate as a fully independent kingdom, although resistance to Mughal authority continued afterwards.

Why the political transition mattered

Independence shifted the principal centre of political decision-making from Delhi to Gujarat. Local rulers could direct military resources, collect revenues, support merchants and commission buildings from their own capitals. Consequently, the rise of the Sultanate was not only a change of dynasty: it also encouraged the development of Ahmedabad, Champaner and other centres of political and economic activity.

Prelims focus

  • 1407: Zafar Khan assumed the title Muzaffar Shah I and established independent rule.
  • 1411: Ahmad Shah I founded Ahmedabad.
  • 1458–1511: Approximate reign of Mahmud Begada.
  • 1472: Mahmud Begada conquered Junagadh.
  • 1484: Mahmud Begada captured Pavagadh and subsequently developed Champaner.
  • 1573: Gujarat came under Mughal rule following Akbar's conquest.
  • Trap: Muzaffar Shah I founded the independent Sultanate; Ahmad Shah I founded Ahmedabad.

[NCERT, Our Pasts–II, Class 7, 2020–21 edition, Chapter 3, The Delhi Sultans, p. 42; Encyclopaedia Iranica, Gujarat, History section, accessed 19 November 2026; Gazetteer of the Bombay Presidency, Volume I, Part I, History of Gujarat, Chapter 12, Introduction, accessed 19 November 2026; UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Historic City of Ahmadabad, Brief Synthesis, accessed 19 November 2026.]

title: Rise of the Gujarat Sultanate: Foundation and Chronology

body:
The foundation of a new capital in 1411

Ahmad Shah I founded Ahmedabad in 1411 on the eastern bank of the Sabarmati River. Before Ahmedabad became the principal capital, Patan, historically known as Anahilwara or Anhilwad Patan, had been a major political centre of Gujarat.

The establishment of Ahmedabad brought together the functions of a royal capital and an expanding commercial town. A capital needed protected residences, administrative establishments, places for public gatherings, religious buildings, markets and routes through which goods could enter the city.

The principal elements of the early city

Bhadra Fort: The royal and military centre

Bhadra Fort was an early structure of Ahmad Shah's new capital. Located near the Sabarmati River, it formed the fortified royal centre. A fort protected important officials, royal establishments and military resources, while also visibly expressing the authority of the sultan.

The fort was developed further under later rulers. Its earliest construction is associated with Ahmad Shah I, while major expansion and completion occurred during Mahmud Begada's reign.

Maidan-e-Shahi and Teen Darwaza

The Maidan-e-Shahi was a large royal open ground connected with the fortified ceremonial centre. Teen Darwaza, meaning three gateways, formed an important monumental entrance associated with this part of the city.

These structures illustrate the difference between a defensive building and a ceremonial urban space. The fort provided protection and housed royal authority; the open ground and monumental gateways helped organize important public and courtly activities.

Jama Masjid: A major congregational mosque

Jama Masjid, also called Jami Masjid, was constructed under Ahmad Shah I. Construction is dated to 1423–1424, with the mosque completed in 1424. It stands near Teen Darwaza and the Bhadra Fort area.

A congregational mosque is a mosque where worshippers gather for collective prayers, particularly the Friday prayer. Jama Masjid therefore served an important religious and public function within the developing city.

The Ahmedabad mosque is recognized for its spacious courtyard, numerous carved columns and domed prayer hall. Its architecture demonstrates how local construction skills were used in a major Sultanate building.

Why Ahmedabad grew into a commercial centre

The establishment of a capital attracted soldiers, administrators, craftspeople, merchants, religious scholars and service providers. These groups required food, clothing, housing, building materials and other goods. Their presence created demand for markets and craft production.

Ahmedabad also benefited from connections with Gujarat's agricultural hinterland and the maritime trading network centred on ports such as Khambhat. Goods produced inland could reach coastal markets, while imported commodities could move towards the capital and surrounding settlements.

Over time, the city developed closely built residential neighbourhoods, including the gated streets known as pols. These neighbourhoods reflect the longer development of Ahmedabad's urban life; not every surviving residential feature dates from the initial foundation in 1411.

Ahmedabad was an inland capital and commercial centre, not a seaport. Its commercial importance depended partly on connections with Gujarat's coastal ports.

Ahmad Shah's lasting contribution

The principal achievement of Ahmad Shah I was the establishment of a durable urban centre in which political administration, defence, religious patronage and commerce reinforced one another. Ahmedabad continued to develop as a major centre long after his reign.

Prelims focus

  • Founder: Ahmad Shah I.
  • Foundation year: 1411.
  • River: Sabarmati.
  • Fort: Bhadra Fort.
  • Important gateway: Teen Darwaza.
  • Jama Masjid: Completed in 1424 under Ahmad Shah I.
  • Trap: Ahmedabad was an inland capital; Khambhat was a major maritime outlet.

[UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Historic City of Ahmadabad, Brief Synthesis and Authenticity sections, accessed 19 November 2026; UNESCO, Urban Heritage Atlas, Historic City of Ahmedabad, Monumental Architecture section, accessed 19 November 2026; Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation, Heritage City, Jama Masjid, accessed 19 November 2026; NCERT, Our Pasts–II, Class 7, 2020–21 edition, Chapter 6, Towns, Traders and Craftspersons, pp. 75–82.]

title: Ahmad Shah I: Ahmedabad as a Fortified Capital and Commercial City

body:
A ruler associated with territorial consolidation

Mahmud Shah I, popularly called Mahmud Begada, ruled Gujarat from approximately 1458 to 1511. He strengthened the Sultanate's authority and extended its control over important fortified centres.

His best-known territorial achievements were the conquest of Junagadh in 1472 and the capture of Pavagadh in 1484. Both places were strategically valuable because their fortifications helped control surrounding territories and routes.

The 2 famous fort conquests

Junagadh and Girnar

Junagadh is located in the Saurashtra region of Gujarat, near the Girnar hills. It was an established fortified centre before Mahmud Begada's conquest. The Sultan captured Junagadh in 1472, bringing this important stronghold under his authority.

The conquest strengthened Sultanate power in Saurashtra. The significance of Junagadh lay in its fortified position and its role in controlling surrounding territory, not in its being a newly founded capital.

Pavagadh and Champaner

Pavagadh is a fortified hill in the present-day Panchmahal region. Champaner lies at the foot of this hill. The hill fortress and the settlement below were closely connected geographically, but they were not the same place.

Mahmud Begada captured the Pavagadh stronghold in 1484. The conquest allowed him to develop Champaner into a major royal centre and capital.

The name Begada is traditionally associated with the conquest of 2 famous forts: the Junagadh-Girnar stronghold and Pavagadh. This is the commonly taught explanation of the title, although different historical explanations of the nickname also exist.

Champaner becomes a royal capital

Following the conquest of Pavagadh, Mahmud Begada rebuilt and expanded the settlement of Champaner below the hill. The developed capital was also known as Muhammadabad.

Champaner's location combined the defensive advantage of the nearby hill fortress with land suitable for an organized urban settlement. Its royal buildings, mosques, residential areas and water installations served the requirements of a functioning capital.

The Jama Masjid at Champaner is one of the most important surviving monuments associated with this phase. It has a large courtyard, richly carved architectural elements and an impressive prayer hall. The monument is an example of the distinctive combination of Indo-Islamic building forms and regional craftsmanship developed under the Gujarat Sultanate.

Why Champaner's capital phase was comparatively short

Champaner was a major Sultanate capital until 1536. Mughal emperor Humayun captured it in 1535, and the Gujarati capital subsequently returned to Ahmedabad. Champaner then lost much of its former political importance.

Its surviving monuments show that a city could become an important capital because of a ruler's military and administrative decisions and later decline when political circumstances changed.

Prelims focus

  • Mahmud Begada: Mahmud Shah I, ruler of Gujarat.
  • 1472: Conquest of Junagadh in Saurashtra.
  • 1484: Capture of Pavagadh near Champaner.
  • Champaner: Developed as a capital after the Pavagadh conquest.
  • Muhammadabad: Name associated with Mahmud Begada's developed capital at Champaner.
  • 1536: End of Champaner's period as Gujarat's capital.
  • Trap: Pavagadh is the fortified hill; Champaner is the settlement at its foot.

[UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Champaner-Pavagadh Archaeological Park, Brief Synthesis and Criterion (iv), accessed 19 November 2026; Gujarat Tourism, Champaner and Pavagadh Archaeological Park, Brief History, accessed 19 November 2026; Government of Gujarat, Junagadh District, History, accessed 19 November 2026; Gujarat State Disaster Management Authority, Junagadh District Disaster Management Plan, District Profile, accessed 19 November 2026.]

body:
How the Sultanate governed its territory

The sultan was the central political and military authority. He exercised power through nobles, district officers, revenue officials and military commanders. However, the Sultanate did not govern every part of Gujarat in exactly the same way.

Some territories were administered directly through officers acting on behalf of the ruler. Other territories remained under local chiefs who recognized the sultan's superior authority and paid tribute or provided services.

Direct administration means government through officers responsible to the central ruler. Tributary rule means that a local chief retains substantial control over internal affairs but accepts a superior ruler and provides an agreed payment or service.

Territories under direct control

Khalsa and sarkar

The territory directly controlled by the Gujarat sultans included khalsa, or crown domains, administered for the central government. Directly governed territory was organized into districts known as sarkars.

These districts could be administered in 2 principal ways. Some were managed by paid royal officers responsible for maintaining order and collecting revenue. Others were assigned to nobles in return for maintaining military contingents. A military contingent was a body of soldiers that the noble was required to support.

This arrangement connected administration to defence. The ruler needed officers to collect income, while military commanders needed resources to maintain soldiers and protect important routes.

Thanas and thanadars

The Sultanate maintained fortified outposts called thanas. These posts helped supervise sensitive areas and maintain local security. The officer in charge of a thana was called a thanadar and was subordinate to the district administration.

In this medieval context, a thana was a fortified military-administrative outpost. It should not automatically be understood as identical to a present-day police station.

Territories under local chiefs

Some local rulers continued to manage their territories after accepting the Gujarat Sultan's authority. These chiefs were expected to provide tribute, which could take the form of money or service.

The arrangement allowed the sultan to extend political influence without replacing every existing local administrative institution. The chief might continue supervising local cultivation, revenue collection and justice within his territory.

Land revenue and tribute were not the same. Land revenue was collected from agricultural production within a territory. Tribute was an obligation imposed on a subordinate ruler or chief in recognition of the sultan's superior authority.

Revenue collection and the state

Agricultural revenue

Agriculture was an important source of income. Revenue officials collected the state demand through local arrangements that involved cultivators, landholders and village headmen. The amount and methods of collection varied across territories.

In directly governed districts, village and district accounts helped the central administration supervise revenue. Officials were expected to report collections through the administrative hierarchy.

Trade and transit dues

The state also benefited from duties on trade and the movement of goods. Markets, merchants and transport routes therefore had fiscal importance as well as commercial importance.

Revenue helped maintain the court, soldiers, fortifications and administrative establishments. Stronger control over productive land and commercial routes made it easier for the sultan to support military campaigns and urban construction.

A basic administrative distinction

Consider 2 territories. In a directly governed district, a royal officer supervised revenue collection and local security on behalf of the sultan. In a tributary territory, a local chief might continue collecting revenue and administering the area while providing an agreed payment or service to the sultan.

Both territories acknowledged the sultan's authority, but the degree of direct control differed.

Prelims focus

  • Khalsa: Crown territory under direct royal authority.
  • Sarkar: A district of directly governed territory.
  • Thana: A fortified administrative or military outpost.
  • Thanadar: Officer responsible for a thana.
  • Revenue: Derived from agriculture as well as trade-related dues.
  • Tributary chiefs: Could retain internal administration while paying tribute or supplying services.
  • Trap: Tributary control did not necessarily mean direct administration of every village by royal officers.

[Gazetteer of the Bombay Presidency, Volume I, Part I, History of Gujarat, Chapter 12, Introduction, sections 13–20, especially the discussions of Crown Lands, Districts and Fiscal Administration, accessed 19 November 2026; Samira Sheikh, Forging a Region: Sultans, Traders, and Pilgrims in Gujarat, 1200–1500, Chapter 5, Court and State: Evolution of a Regional Consensus, abstract, Oxford University Press, accessed 19 November 2026.]
